# 1 Chronicles 19 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview

This chapter is a near-duplicate of 2 Samuel 10:1–19, recounting David's war with Ammon and their Aramean (Syrian) allies. The Chronicler omits the story of David's kindness to Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 9) as belonging to private rather than public history. The chapter also omits David's sin with Bathsheba — as Gaebelein notes, "David's fall is omitted in Chronicles because the grace of God is the prominent feature and grace had completely covered David's great sin."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/1-chronicles-19.html

The Chronicler devotes considerable space to the Ammonite campaigns because they solidify the "rest" needed for the temple building. Mark Boda notes a key contrast: chapter 18 shows David on the offensive; chapter 19 presents David on the defensive, drawn into war by the arrogant Ammonites and fearful Arameans.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-19-commentary

---

## v. 1: "Some time later, Nahash king of the Ammonites died and was succeeded by his son."

**The phrase "after this"** has no precise chronological significance (Ellicott). It is the second of three such appearances introducing sections in chapters 18–20.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-19.html

**Who was Nahash?** Saul's first military campaign was against Nahash (1 Samuel 11). The Pulpit Commentary notes that if this is the same Nahash, nearly sixty years would have elapsed, making it unlikely. Josephus says that Nahash of 1 Samuel 11 was killed in Saul's destruction of the Ammonite army. The word "Nahash" (meaning "serpent") may have been an official title of Ammonite kings, like "Pharaoh" for Egypt.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-19.html

**August Konkel** suggests that when David came to power, he negotiated terms of agreement with Nahash that maintained peace, probably including taxation revenues. The death of a king could trigger instability since treaties were made between individuals.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-19-commentary

---

## v. 2: "And David said, 'I will show kindness to Hanun son of Nahash, because his father showed kindness to me.' So David sent messengers to console Hanun concerning his father."

**The Hebrew word for "kindness" is *hesed*** — covenant loyalty, faithful love in action. Precept Austin notes this word has covenant connotations and "may imply some sort of informal treaty between David and Nahash." David was extending an olive branch, seeking to renew the covenantal agreement.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-19-commentary

**What kindness did Nahash show David?** The specific instance is not recorded in Scripture. The Pulpit Commentary suggests that during David's fugitive years, when Saul was pursuing him, Nahash — as Saul's enemy — had motive to show kindness to David. The relationship is "best explained by their common hostility toward Saul" (Selman, cited by Andrew Hill). Remarkably, a genuine kindliness towards David still clung to the Ammonite succession even after the events of this chapter (see 2 Samuel 17:27–29, where Shobi son of Nahash brought provisions to David).
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-19-commentary; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-19.html

**David's kindness was active, not passive.** Guzik emphasizes: "David wasn't content to feel kindness towards Hanun. He did something to bring the grieving man comfort."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-19/

---

## v. 3: "The princes of the Ammonites said to Hanun, 'Just because David has sent you comforters, do you really believe he is showing respect for your father? Have not his servants come to you to explore the land, spy it out, and overthrow it?'"

**Suspicion poisons everything.** Matthew Henry calls this "great incivility to David." The Pulpit Commentary devotes an entire homiletic section to "the ill work of suspiciousness," calling suspicion a "little shuttle" that weaves "unmitigated mischief." It notes two conspiring causes: (1) bad advisers feeding on suspicion, and (2) the weakness of the ruling head who should have overruled them.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-19.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/1-chronicles-19.html

**Guzik** observes: "It is common for liars to always suspect others of lying." The princes may have genuinely suspected David or simply used this to appear cunning to the new king.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-19/

**The NET Bible notes** a textual issue: the Hebrew verb *lahafokh* ("to overthrow") seems misplaced in the sequence of three infinitives. Some scholars emend it to *lakhpor* ("to spy out"), suggesting a conflation of alternative readings. The parallel passage in 2 Samuel reads "to search the city" rather than "the land."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-19-commentary

---

## v. 4: "So Hanun took David's servants, shaved their beards, cut off their garments at the hips, and sent them away."

**The cultural enormity of shaving the beard.** Keil and Delitzsch write: "With the value universally set upon the beard by the Hebrews and other Oriental nations, as being man's greatest ornament, the cutting off of one-half of it was the greatest insult that could have been offered to the ambassadors, and through them to David their king." Adam Clarke adds that in the East a man "considers it his greatest ornament; often swears by it; and, in matters of great importance, pledges it. Nothing can be more secure than a pledge of this kind; its owner will redeem it at the hazard of his life." A clean-shaven face was the mark of a slave; free men wore beards.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-19/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-19-commentary

**Forcing Israelites to violate Torah.** Bergen notes that to remove an Israelite male's beard forcibly was to force him to violate the Torah (Leviticus 19:27) and show contempt for him personally. Likewise, cutting the garments made them unacceptable by Torah standards (Numbers 15:38; Deuteronomy 22:12).
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-19-commentary

**Cutting garments at the hips** (literally "cut their robes in the middle unto their buttocks") was also a deep humiliation. Adam Clarke comments that this exposed "the shame of their nakedness…and especially that of their circumcision, so derided by the heathen." John Trapp (Puritan) added a pointed application: "This is check to the fashion-mongers of our time, saith Piscator; who wear their clothes so close, and cloaks so short, that they cover not their buttocks."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-19/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-19-commentary

**Walton** (IVP Background Commentary) notes this was a "symbolic castration" — an act of war. What seems like a "prank" was in fact a direct challenge to David's power and authority, precipitating war.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-19-commentary

**To insult the ambassador is to insult the king.** Guzik draws a parallel to Jesus and His ambassadors: "If the world hates you, you know that it hated Me before it hated you" (John 15:18).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-19/

---

## v. 5: "When someone came and told David about his men, he sent messengers to meet them, since the men had been thoroughly humiliated. The king told them, 'Stay in Jericho until your beards have grown back, and then return.'"

**David's pastoral care for his men.** Rather than using these humiliated men as political tools to whip up anger against Ammon, David cared first for their personal dignity. Precept Austin calls this "another mark of a man after God's own heart."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-19/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-19-commentary

**Why Jericho?** Bob Utley notes Jericho was one of the most ancient cities, not large during this period, on the border of Israel and Ammon but on the western side of the Jordan — "a good, quiet, insignificant place for these men to regrow their beards."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-19-commentary

---

## v. 6: "When the Ammonites realized that they had become a stench to David, Hanun and the Ammonites sent a thousand talents of silver to hire for themselves chariots and horsemen from Aram-naharaim, Aram-maacah, and Zobah."

**"Made themselves odious"** — the Hebrew root *ba'ash* is very strong, meaning "to stink." The Pulpit Commentary notes the Authorized Version translates it more bluntly elsewhere.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-19.html

**A thousand talents of silver** — this amount is not stated in the parallel passage (2 Samuel 10:6). The Pulpit Commentary estimates a talent as equivalent to about £342 (in 19th-century currency), making this a massive expenditure. The Ammonites hired mercenaries from three regions: Aram-naharaim (Mesopotamia, "Syria of the Two Rivers"), Aram-maacah (north of East Manasseh), and Zobah.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-19.html

**The parallel passage** (2 Samuel 10:6) adds "the men of Ishtob" and specifies numbers: 20,000 foot soldiers from Beth-rehob and Zobah, 1,000 men from Maacah, and 12,000 from Tob.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-19-commentary

---

## v. 7: "So they hired for themselves thirty-two thousand chariots, as well as the king of Maacah with his troops, who came and camped near Medeba while the Ammonites came from their cities and marched out for battle."

**The thirty-two thousand** is a number of fighting men, not chariots. The Pulpit Commentary notes that "a stop should follow the numeral, which designates the number of the men under arms" — matching the 32,000 total in the 2 Samuel 10 parallel.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-19.html

**Medeba** — a city about four miles southeast of Heshbon (Numbers 21:30; Joshua 13:9, 16; Isaiah 15:2). Not mentioned in the Samuel parallel.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-19.html

---

## v. 8: "On hearing this, David sent Joab and the entire army of mighty men."

**Joab** commanded "the entire army of mighty men." Guzik notes that David was nothing without his mighty men, and they were nothing without him. Many of these men didn't start as mighty — they were the distressed, indebted, and discontented who followed David at Adullam Cave (1 Samuel 22:1–2).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-19/

---

## v. 9: "The Ammonites marched out and arrayed themselves for battle at the entrance to the city, while the kings who had come stayed by themselves in the open country."

**Tactical positioning.** The Ammonites positioned themselves at the gate of Rabbah (their capital), while the mercenary Aramean kings took position some distance away in the open field. This created a pincer situation: Joab would have enemies both in front of him and behind him.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-19/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-19.html

Lange's Commentary notes the reading "at the entrance to the city" (פֶּתַח הָעִיר) is to be preferred as clearer than 2 Samuel's "at the entrance of the gate."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lcc/1-chronicles-19.html

---

## vv. 10–11: Joab divides his forces — best men against the Arameans, the rest under Abishai against the Ammonites.

**Joab faced a battle on two fronts.** Ellicott notes: "The battle was set against him before and behind — literally, the front of the battle had become towards him, front and rear." The Ammonites lay in front of the city; their Aramean allies were at some distance in the plain. To attack either with his entire army would expose his rear to the other.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-19.html

**Joab took the "choice of Israel"** (literally, the chosen or young warriors) against the Arameans as the stronger and "most dangerous enemy," while sending his brother Abishai against the Ammonites.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-19.html

**Kingcomments** (Ger de Koning) notes: "Joab oversees the situation and notices that he is enclosed. That doesn't cause him to panic. As an experienced general with great military insight he determines a tactic."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/1-chronicles-19.html

---

## v. 12: "'If the Arameans are too strong for me,' said Joab, 'then you will come to my rescue. And if the Ammonites are too strong for you, then I will come to your rescue.'"

**Mutual support pact.** Guzik notes: "Joab had only one strategy in battle — attack. Many generals would consider surrender when surrounded on both sides by the enemy, but not Joab." Morgan observes it is "interesting that in his arrangements he made no allowance for the possibility of ultimate defeat…it does not seem to have occurred to him that the combination might have been too much for both of them."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-19/

**Matthew Henry** remarks: "How the courage of brave men is heightened and invigorated by difficulties. When Joab saw that the battle was set against him before and behind, instead of meditating a retreat, he doubled his resolution."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/1-chronicles-19.html

---

## v. 13: "'Be strong and let us fight bravely for our people and for the cities of our God. May the LORD do what is good in His sight.'"

**Three elements of Joab's speech**, per Guzik: (1) **Courage and strength are choices**, not feelings — "we can be strong in the Lord and in the power of His might" (Ephesians 6:10). (2) **They fought for something bigger than themselves** — "for our people and for the cities of our God." (3) **They entrusted the outcome to God** — "May the LORD do what is good in His sight." Guzik cites F.B. Meyer: "To believe that God will do all, and therefore to do nothing, is as bad as to believe that God leaves us to our unaided endeavours."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-19/

**Precept Austin** highlights the "mysterious (but very real) juxtaposition of Joab and Abishai doing their part (man's responsibility) while at the same time trusting in Yahweh's goodness (God's sovereignty)."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-19-commentary

**The Pulpit Commentary homily** on this verse treats it as a description of "true valour": the heart of the valiant (courage), the conduct of the valiant (brave deeds), the motive of the valiant ("for our people"), and the confidence of the valiant ("let the Lord do what is good").
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-19.html

**Ellicott** notes that the Chronicler lays stress on the word "good," and on "Jehovah" as the one who is Lord of hosts and God of battles. "Evidently the spirit which inspired the prayer, 'Thy will be done,' was not unknown to the warriors of the old theocracy."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-19.html

**Lange** adds: "For our people, and for the city of our God: that these may not fall into the hands of the heathen, and from cities of the Lord become cities of idols."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lcc/1-chronicles-19.html

---

## vv. 14–15: "So Joab and his troops advanced to fight the Arameans, who fled before him. When the Ammonites saw that the Arameans had fled, they too fled before Joab's brother Abishai, and they entered the city. So Joab went back to Jerusalem."

**The enemy fled without a full battle.** Guzik notes: "It doesn't even say that Joab engaged the Syrians in battle. This mercenary army fled before the army of the mighty men because God was with them. God promised this kind of blessing upon an obedient Israel (Deuteronomy 28:7)."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-19/

**The Ammonites retreated into Rabbah.** Joab did not at once besiege the city. Payne suggests "it may have been too late in the year." The Pulpit Commentary says Joab "did not stay to besiege the Ammonites in the city, within the walls of which they had taken refuge, nor to pursue the Syrians. Hence we find these latter soon made bold to rally."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-19/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-19.html

---

## v. 16: "When the Arameans saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they sent messengers to bring more Arameans from beyond the Euphrates, with Shophach the commander of Hadadezer's army leading them."

**The Syrians would not quit after one defeat.** They called reinforcements from "beyond the River" (the Euphrates) — described as a persistent enemy who "came back to fight again" (Guzik). The Pulpit Commentary notes that the earlier forces from Mesopotamia may have been only partial or not truly representative of the region, and now fuller forces from beyond the Euphrates were summoned.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-19/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-19.html

**Shophach** is spelled Shobach in 2 Samuel 10:16. Nothing else is known of him except his death in v. 18.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-19.html

---

## v. 17: "When this was reported to David, he gathered all Israel, crossed the Jordan, advanced toward the Arameans, and arrayed for battle against them. When David lined up to engage them in battle, they fought against him."

**David himself now takes the field.** This is a significant escalation. The parallel passage in 2 Samuel says they came to "Helam," a location otherwise unknown. The Septuagint has Αἰλάμ.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-19.html

**The emphasis on "all Israel"** is important to the Chronicler. Selman (cited by Guzik) notes: "The whole incident therefore shows 'all Israel' cooperating under David and establishing the required 'rest' for building the temple."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-19/

**Guzik** observes a poignant warning: "We see in 2 Samuel 10 that God gave David a warning by showing it necessary for him to come out against the Syrians. David tried to leave the battle to Joab…but his army needed him and God tried to show him that by blessing it when David did go out to battle. These events were God's gracious warning that David sadly wasted." This foreshadows David's fatal decision to stay in Jerusalem during the next spring's campaign, leading to his sin with Bathsheba.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-19/

---

## v. 18: "But the Arameans fled before Israel, and David killed seven thousand of their charioteers and forty thousand foot soldiers. He also killed Shophach the commander of their army."

**Numbers discrepancy.** The parallel passage (2 Samuel 10:18) has "700 chariots" rather than "7,000 charioteers" (or "men which fought in chariots"). The Pulpit Commentary suggests the Samuel reading is more likely correct, observing "there could not be ten fighting men to a chariot." Matthew Henry reconciles the numbers by noting: "as now in a man of war for sea-service they allot ten men to a gun, so then, in land-service, ten men to a chariot." The 2 Samuel passage also reads "horsemen" rather than "foot soldiers."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-19.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/1-chronicles-19.html

---

## v. 19: "When Hadadezer's subjects saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they made peace with David and became subject to him. So the Arameans were unwilling to help the Ammonites anymore."

**Transfer of allegiance.** The Pulpit Commentary notes a characteristic difference between Chronicles and Samuel: the parallel passage says the kings "made peace with Israel" and "served them," while Chronicles says they "made peace with David" and "became his servants." "To the writer of Samuel God's people is the main topic; to the chronicler the divinely-anointed king."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-19.html

**Matthew Henry** draws a spiritual lesson: "those who have meddled with strife that belongs not to them, and have found that they meddled to their own hurt, do well to learn wit at length and meddle no further…Let those who have in vain stood it out against God be thus wise for themselves, and agree with him quickly, while they are in the way. Let them become his servants; for they cannot but see themselves undone if they be his enemies."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/1-chronicles-19.html

**Morgan** notes the chapter ends with unfinished business at Rabbah — the offending Ammonites still in their city and Joab returned to Jerusalem. "Victory is in itself a peril to any man…Constant watchfulness is the only guarantee of safety. Not even true desire and great blessing are sufficient if the heart be not personally watchful."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gcm/1-chronicles-19.html

---

## Points of Tradition-Specific Interest

### Reformed / Covenant Theology
The use of *hesed* (covenant loyalty/lovingkindness) in v. 2 is significant for Reformed covenant theology. Precept Austin provides an extensive word study showing how *hesed* denotes "God's no-strings-attached covenant loyalty," parallel to the NT term *agapē*. David's *hesed* to Hanun reflects the covenant faithfulness God shows His people. The Chronicler's focus on the Davidic king (v. 19 — "became his servants" vs. Samuel's "served them") reflects a theocratic, Davidic-covenant perspective.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-19-commentary

### Baptist (Particular/Reformed Baptist)
John Gill's commentary simply refers the reader to his notes on 2 Samuel 10, noting "very little variations." The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary was listed in search results but could not be fully retrieved. Gill's approach reflects the historic Baptist emphasis on the unity of Scripture and careful comparison of parallel passages.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-chronicles-19.html

### Methodist / Holiness
The Pulpit Commentary's homiletics section (by W. Clarkson) treats the chapter as "a bundle of mistakes" and "the ill work of suspiciousness," drawing moral and practical lessons about counsel, charity vs. suspicion, and the consequences of insult — very much in the Methodist homiletical tradition of practical holiness teaching. Clarkson's point V — "that persistency prevails when we fight against God" — echoes the Wesleyan emphasis on submission to God's will.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-19.html (Homiletics section)

### Pentecostal / Charismatic
David Guzik (Enduring Word, broadly charismatic) emphasizes Joab's speech in v. 13 as "pure faith," balancing preparation with trust in God's supernatural intervention. He also highlights the practical working of spiritual warfare principles and the necessity of the Holy Spirit's empowerment for spiritual vigilance.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-19/

### Dispensational
Gaebelein's Annotated Bible emphasizes the Chronicler's omission of David's sin with Bathsheba as a demonstration that "the grace of God is the prominent feature" — grace having "completely covered David's great sin." He also notes the typological importance of "all Israel" being gathered under David, pointing toward future unity under the Messianic king.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/1-chronicles-19.html

### Lutheran
I was unable to retrieve specific Lutheran commentary from lcms.org or 1517.org within the available searches on this chapter.

### Modern Scholarship
The NET Bible notes (cited by Precept Austin) address a textual issue in v. 3 regarding the Hebrew verb *lahafokh* ("to overthrow"), which seems misplaced in the sequence; some scholars emend to *lakhpor* ("to spy out"). The IVP Bible Background Commentary (Walton, cited by Precept Austin) provides extensive cultural background on beard-shaving as symbolic emasculation, the cutting of garments as treatment reserved for slaves and captives, and comparisons to Assyrian royal annals where violations of sworn agreements justified declarations of war.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-19-commentary

---

**Summary of the chapter's spiritual message:** David's kindness was repaid with suspicion and insult, leading to a war in which God gave Israel victory. The chapter teaches that suspicion destroys relationships, that courage must be paired with trust in God's sovereignty, and that unfinished business (Rabbah) can become the occasion for later moral disaster — as G. Campbell Morgan warned, "Constant watchfulness is the only guarantee of safety."
